screens.title: State Machines & Singletons
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two practical patterns that keep your Unity codebase healthy as projects grow: the State Machine and the Singleton. The State Machine gives objects clear, encapsulated modes such as Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and Dead, so behavior is explicit and easier to extend. The Singleton gives a single, globally accessible instance for managers like game state and scoring, so scripts can reach shared services without messy find calls or tangled references. You will see concrete C# starter code that uses an enum and a switch for a simple enemy AI, then a Singleton manager for player score. Along the way we’ll surface common pitfalls — such as sprawling Update methods, accidentally creating multiple Singletons, and coupling your logic too tightly to global state. Why this matters: projects that adopt these patterns early avoid “spaghetti” Update loops and become easier to debug, test, and extend. As you follow the code walkthroughs and the hands-on activity, notice how each pattern improves readability and where trade-offs appear. By the end, you’ll be able to implement both patterns and choose where each belongs in your game architecture.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what a State Machine is, implement a simple one in C#, describe the Singleton pattern and build a Singleton manager in Unity. You’ll practice a concrete enemy AI that uses states like Idle, Chase, and Attack, and you’ll implement a PlayerScoreManager Singleton that persists across scenes. These are practical skills: state machines avoid complex nested conditionals and make behaviors modular, and Singletons let you access key services from anywhere without repeated lookups. A frequent misconception is that Singletons are always bad; in fact, they are appropriate for a truly unique, globally used manager — but they should be applied sparingly because of test and coupling concerns. The objectives emphasize both implementation and judgement: learn how these patterns work, implement starter code safely, and identify scenarios where each pattern improves maintainability. screens.title: What is a State Machine?
screens.narratorSegment: A State Machine defines a finite set of named modes an object can be in, and it pairs each mode with behavior and explicit transitions. In games, a character or enemy uses states such as Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and Dead; each state encapsulates what the object does while in that mode and what conditions move it to another mode. The key benefit is separation: instead of one large Update method full of nested checks, each state holds its own logic, which makes code easier to read, test, and extend. A concrete example is an enemy that patrols until it detects the player, then switches to Chase; when close enough it switches to Attack, and if health hits zero it becomes Dead. A common misconception is that a State Machine always requires complex frameworks — for many cases an enum plus a switch statement is clear and sufficient. For larger AI systems you might move to an interface-based IState with separate classes, but begin with the enum approach to learn transition concepts. Takeaway: prefer explicit states and transitions over sprawling conditional logic; ask whether a behavior belongs in a dedicated state or as a condition inside another state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › State Machine
Definition & Purpose
A finite set of states with actions and transitions that keep behavior predictable.
Why use one?
  • Encapsulates logic per state so single methods don’t grow large.
  • Makes transitions explicit and testable.
  • Eases adding new behaviors without breaking existing ones.
Common mistake
Filling Update with many nested ifs; prefer states instead.
Key takeaway
Start simple: an enum and switch are valid for small agents. Move to class-based states as complexity grows.
Concrete example: enemy modes
State list
Idle — wait and scan
Patrol — follow waypoints
Chase — move toward player
Attack — deal damage
Dead — play death and cleanup
Example code (enum + switch)
// Define possible states
public enum EnemyState { Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, Dead }

// In a MonoBehaviour
public EnemyState currentState = EnemyState.Idle;

void Update()
{
  switch (currentState)
  {
    case EnemyState.Idle:
      HandleIdleState();
      break;
    case EnemyState.Patrol:
      HandlePatrolState();
      break;
    // ... other states
  }
}
Analogy
Think of a traffic light: each color is a state with rules for when to switch to the next color.
Key Takeaway

Use explicit states to simplify behavior and make transitions clear and testable.

screens.title: Enum + Switch: a simple State Machine implementation
screens.narratorSegment: We’ll walk through the enum-and-switch pattern for SimpleEnemyAI, a clean starting point for learning state-driven behavior. The enemy uses an EnemyState enum that lists Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and sometimes Dead. In Update the switch calls state handlers like HandleIdleState, HandleChaseState, and HandleAttackState. Each handler contains the state-specific logic and sets currentState when a transition occurs, for example when the player enters detectionRange the Idle handler sets currentState to Chase. A concrete run: the enemy starts Idle, it detects the Player and changes to Chase, it approaches until within attackRange and sets Attack, then when the player moves away it returns to Chase or Idle. A common misconception is expecting the switch to handle timing and animation; the switch only routes behavior — timers, cooldowns, and animation blending remain responsibilities inside the state handlers. When you test, look at Debug. Log outputs to verify state changes and use clear guard conditions so states don’t flip rapidly. Question to ponder: if your AI needs many shared utilities, does splitting states into IState classes improve clarity? Try refactoring when logic grows. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Enum + Switch Walkthrough
Starter code: switch-based State Machine
A readable pattern for small AI components
public enum EnemyState { Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, Dead }

public class EnemyAI : MonoBehaviour
{
  public EnemyState currentState = EnemyState.Idle;

  void Update()
  {
    switch (currentState)
    {
      case EnemyState.Idle:
        HandleIdleState();
        break;
      case EnemyState.Patrol:
        HandlePatrolState();
        break;
      case EnemyState.Chase:
        HandleChaseState();
        break;
      case EnemyState.Attack:
        HandleAttackState();
        break;
      case EnemyState.Dead:
        HandleDeadState();
        break;
    }
  }

  void HandleIdleState() { /* ... */ }
  void HandlePatrolState() { /* ... */ }
  void HandleChaseState() { /* ... */ }
  void HandleAttackState() { /* ... */ }
  void HandleDeadState() { /* ... */ }
}
Explanation
  • Current state: stored in currentState, determines behavior routing.
  • Handlers: each method contains state-specific logic and performs transitions.
  • Transitions: set currentState explicitly when conditions are met (e.g., detectionRange).
Example scenario
Enemy in Idle detects player at distance under detectionRange, sets state to Chase, then enters Attack when within attackRange.
Key Takeaway

Use guard conditions inside handlers and log transitions to avoid rapid state hopping.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › SimpleEnemyAI
Complete example (excerpt)
using UnityEngine;

public enum EnemyState { Idle, Chase, Attack }

public class SimpleEnemyAI : MonoBehaviour
{
  public EnemyState currentState = EnemyState.Idle;
  public float detectionRange = 10f;
  public float attackRange = 2f;
  public float moveSpeed = 3f;
  public float attackCooldown = 1f;

  private Transform playerTransform;
  private float lastAttackTime;

  void Start()
  {
    GameObject player = GameObject.FindWithTag("Player");
    if (player != null) playerTransform = player.transform;
    else Debug.LogError("Player GameObject with tag 'Player' not found!");
  }

  void Update()
  {
    if (playerTransform == null) return;
    switch (currentState) { /* handlers */ }
  }

  void HandleIdleState() { /* detect and set Chase */ }
  void HandleChaseState() { /* move toward player, check attackRange */ }
  void HandleAttackState() { /* perform attack with cooldown and add score */ }
}
Testing checklist
  • Ensure Player has the tag "Player" and a Transform.
  • Watch console logs for Idle → Chase → Attack transitions.
  • Confirm PlayerScoreManager.Instance is available before calling AddScore.
Pro tip
Keep movement and physics consistent with your project: modify Rigidbody for physics-based movement, not transform, when using physics interactions.
Key Takeaway

Log state changes and verify guard checks to avoid rapid or unintended transitions.

screens.title: What is a Singleton?
screens.narratorSegment: A Singleton ensures only one instance of a class exists and provides a global access point, usually via a static Instance property. In Unity, Singletons are commonly used for managers that truly must be unique and reachable from any script: game flow managers, audio managers, or a centralized PlayerScoreManager. The canonical Unity pattern checks in Awake if an Instance already exists and destroys duplicates, sets Instance to this if not, and often calls DontDestroyOnLoad to persist across scene loads. A concrete example from the chapter is GameManager with a static Instance and a CurrentScore property; Awake enforces uniqueness and DontDestroyOnLoad keeps it alive. A common misconception is to overuse Singletons as a shortcut for passing references; this can introduce global state that makes unit tests and component reuse harder. Use Singletons sparingly, for services that truly require single-instance, and document why a class is a Singleton. Closing question: which managers in your project truly need global, single-instance access versus local references or dependency injection? What is a Singleton? means singletons solve access problems but add global state; reserve them for truly unique, globally needed services.. In practical terms, a single instance and a global access point for manager classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Singleton
Singleton pattern in Unity
Ensure one instance and provide global access.
public class GameManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  public static GameManager Instance { get; private set; }
  public int CurrentScore { get; private set; } = 0;

  void Awake()
  {
    if (Instance != null && Instance != this)
    {
      Destroy(gameObject); // prevent duplicates
    }
    else
    {
      Instance = this;
      DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }
  }

  public void AddScore(int amount) { CurrentScore += amount; }
}
When to use
  • Use for managers that must be unique and widely available.
  • Avoid for tightly scoped systems that can accept injected references.
  • Guard Awake to destroy duplicates and consider persistence with DontDestroyOnLoad.
Pitfall
Global Singletons can hide dependencies and make unit testing difficult.
Key Takeaway

Favor Singletons only for truly global services; document their role and guard against duplicates.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › PlayerScoreManager
Starter Singleton code
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerScoreManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  public static PlayerScoreManager Instance { get; private set; }
  public int CurrentScore { get; private set; } = 0;

  void Awake()
  {
    if (Instance != null && Instance != this)
    {
      Destroy(gameObject);
    }
    else
    {
      Instance = this;
      DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
      Debug.Log("PlayerScoreManager Singleton initialized.");
    }
  }

  public void AddScore(int amount)
  {
    CurrentScore += amount;
    Debug.Log($"Score updated: {CurrentScore}");
  }

  public void ResetScore()
  {
    CurrentScore = 0;
    Debug.Log("Score reset.");
  }
}
How other scripts call it
PlayerScoreManager.Instance?.AddScore(1); // safe call if not null
Practical notes
  • Attach to an empty GameObject named GameManagers.
  • Verify only one instance in the scene hierarchy.

screens.title: Designing transitions and guards
screens.narratorSegment: Transitions are the rules that move an object from one state to another, and guard conditions keep those transitions stable. For example, your enemy’s Idle handler might check if Vector3. Distance to the player is less than detectionRange and then set currentState to Chase. Guards prevent quick oscillations: use hysteresis, cooldown timers, or widen thresholds so small movements don’t flip state repeatedly. The Attack handler commonly uses a cooldown to prevent continuous attacks; this is implemented with lastAttackTime and attackCooldown. Another practical pattern is to use explicit Enter and Exit actions for states to set or clear timers and animation flags. A common misconception is that transitions should be checked only in one place; while centralized checks are possible, placing the condition inside the active state handler makes reasoning about behavior local and testable. Example: when health is low, set a Flee state rather than patching health checks into multiple handlers. Closing question: what guard or cooldown would you add to your AI to prevent it from rapidly switching between Chase and Attack? screens.title: Combining patterns: AI reporting to a Game Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Combining a State Machine AI with a Singleton manager is a common and useful architecture. The AI remains responsible for local behavior while the Singleton provides globally required services like score, audio triggers, or scene transitions. For example, when the enemy’s Attack handler registers a successful hit or the enemy dies, it calls PlayerScoreManager. Instance. AddScore to update global score. This keeps the AI decoupled from UI or scene logic: the enemy does not need to know how the score is displayed, only that the manager accepts an AddScore call. A frequent misconception is that this coupling makes the AI hard to reuse; in fact, the coupling is limited: the AI depends on a known manager interface but not on its implementation details. If you want testability, wrap global calls behind an interface or event system so unit tests can substitute a mock manager. Closing question: if you needed to report many event types from many agents, would you use the Singleton directly or introduce an event bus or service interface instead? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two practical patterns that keep your Unity codebase healthy as projects grow: the State Machine and the Singleton. The State Machine gives objects clear, encapsulated modes such as Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and Dead, so behavior is explicit and easier to extend. The Singleton gives a single, globally accessible instance for managers like game state and scoring, so scripts can reach shared services without messy find calls or tangled references. You will see concrete C# starter code that uses an enum and a switch for a simple enemy AI, then a Singleton manager for player score. Along the way we’ll surface common pitfalls — such as sprawling Update methods, accidentally creating multiple Singletons, and coupling your logic too tightly to global state. Why this matters: projects that adopt these patterns early avoid “spaghetti” Update loops and become easier to debug, test, and extend. As you follow the code walkthroughs and the hands-on activity, notice how each pattern improves readability and where trade-offs appear. By the end, you’ll be able to implement both patterns and choose where each belongs in your game architecture.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what a State Machine is, implement a simple one in C#, describe the Singleton pattern and build a Singleton manager in Unity. You’ll practice a concrete enemy AI that uses states like Idle, Chase, and Attack, and you’ll implement a PlayerScoreManager Singleton that persists across scenes. These are practical skills: state machines avoid complex nested conditionals and make behaviors modular, and Singletons let you access key services from anywhere without repeated lookups. A frequent misconception is that Singletons are always bad; in fact, they are appropriate for a truly unique, globally used manager — but they should be applied sparingly because of test and coupling concerns. The objectives emphasize both implementation and judgement: learn how these patterns work, implement starter code safely, and identify scenarios where each pattern improves maintainability. Prepare to code, observe runtime transitions, and reflect on where each pattern fits in your architecture.

These objectives extend the practical skills: you will learn to connect a State Machine-based AI with a Singleton manager and to identify scenarios where each pattern improves organization and maintainability. The chapter explicitly points out the need to avoid large nested if-else chains in Update methods by placing logic per state, and to avoid overusing Singletons where local references suffice. You will implement a SimpleEnemyAI with Patrol, Chase, and Attack states, and a PlayerScoreManager Singleton that updates when the enemy attacks or is defeated. Important misconceptions are highlighted: do not assume Singletons fix all reference issues — they introduce global state that can make unit tests harder. Also, a basic enum-and-switch is fine for simple AI, but larger systems may benefit from an interface-based IState approach for separation of concerns. Practically, you will follow starter code, run the scene, and observe console logs and score updates. These exercises teach both syntax and design judgment so you can choose the right pattern in your next Unity project.

A State Machine defines a finite set of named modes an object can be in, and it pairs each mode with behavior and explicit transitions. In games, a character or enemy uses states such as Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and Dead; each state encapsulates what the object does while in that mode and what conditions move it to another mode. The key benefit is separation: instead of one large Update method full of nested checks, each state holds its own logic, which makes code easier to read, test, and extend. A concrete example is an enemy that patrols until it detects the player, then switches to Chase; when close enough it switches to Attack, and if health hits zero it becomes Dead. A common misconception is that a State Machine always requires complex frameworks — for many cases an enum plus a switch statement is clear and sufficient. For larger AI systems you might move to an interface-based IState with separate classes, but begin with the enum approach to learn transition concepts. Takeaway: prefer explicit states and transitions over sprawling conditional logic; ask whether a behavior belongs in a dedicated state or as a condition inside another state.

We’ll walk through the enum-and-switch pattern for SimpleEnemyAI, a clean starting point for learning state-driven behavior. The enemy uses an EnemyState enum that lists Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and sometimes Dead. In Update the switch calls state handlers like HandleIdleState, HandleChaseState, and HandleAttackState. Each handler contains the state-specific logic and sets currentState when a transition occurs, for example when the player enters detectionRange the Idle handler sets currentState to Chase. A concrete run: the enemy starts Idle, it detects the Player and changes to Chase, it approaches until within attackRange and sets Attack, then when the player moves away it returns to Chase or Idle. A common misconception is expecting the switch to handle timing and animation; the switch only routes behavior — timers, cooldowns, and animation blending remain responsibilities inside the state handlers. When you test, look at Debug. Log outputs to verify state changes and use clear guard conditions so states don’t flip rapidly. In Chase the enemy moves toward the player and switches to Attack when within attackRange, or back to Idle if the player moves far away. Let’s recap the essential ideas. First, State Machines divide object behavior into distinct states with clear transitions and encapsulated logic. This reduces conditional complexity and improves maintainability. Second, a Singleton ensures a single instance and a global point of access, useful for managers that truly must be unique, but it introduces global state and potential testing issues. Third, combine these patterns carefully: have your AI manage behavior with states and report events to a well-defined manager, using interfaces or event buses when you need better testability.
